newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish zloty crawl favourable for exports - Belka.
newsitem.headline: Polish zloty crawl favourable for exports - Belka.

text.p: Poland's Finance Minister Marek Belka said on Wednesday the current pace of the crawling peg devaluation of the zloty was favourable for exporters and there was no need for the currency's deeper depreciation.

Belka told a news conference the present monthly devaluation rate of one percent has exceeded over the last several months the growth of producer prices, which meant profitability of exports was improving.
"The zloty is devalued by one percent a mongh while over the last several months the growth of producer prices has remained below one percent and it was 0.6 percent in February," Belka said.
"So from the point of view of exporters the situation is not worsening but improving," he added.

The yawning $1.48 billion trade deficit in January has renewed concerns over Poland's widening trade gap and provoked suggestions from exporters and some political groups that the zloty's devaluation should be deeper.

The junior party in the ruling coalition, the Polish Peasant Party, as well as the opposition Movement for Reconstruction of Poland (ROP) have been criticising the current exchange rate policy, saying it is harming exports.
But Belka reiterated that the trade deficit was a natural side-effect of Poland's fast economic growth, booming foreign investment and fast investment spending.
"Countries which experience a period of fast growth, fast modernisation and record annual investment growth of about 20 percent...all are recording trade deficits," he said.

Belka said that the strong dollar might be negatively affecting firms exporting to Germany or other European countries but this had more to do with trends on world currency markets than with Poland's exchange rate policy.

He also said that Poland could reduce its dependence on the pace of economic growth in European Union countries and Germany in particular, which accounts for about 30 percent of Poland's exports, by seeking new opportunities east of its border.
"It's true that European Union economies are less dynamic than the U.S. or Asian ones but our chance is in...expansion onto the former Soviet Union," he said.
He said that although Russia has yet to rebound and show growth, its eventual recovery would offer attractive opportunities to Polish companies.
